It is noteworthy that free bases do not adhere to the same properties observed in abelian groups, exhibiting more complex behavior. Although individual behavior is a primary driver of virus transmission, it is also influenced by what information others share about the virus.  This paper develops a mathematical model that accounts for both individual behavior and the spread of viruses in an evolving social network.  The model considers a simple, yet significant aspect of virus transmission:  the difference between rumors and genuine infections.  Specifically, the model distinguishes between people who have heard about the virus, including those who have not been infected, and those who have not heard about it at all.  The model also includes a delay equation that represents the spread of viruses in an evolving population, in addition to an epidemic threshold that indicates whether the virus will spread rapidly or die out quickly.  The results of the model's analysis provide valuable insights into the impact of NPIs, the spread of viruses in an evolving population, and the influence of rumors on the spread of these viruses.  The model's numerical solutions are demonstrated through case studies about the spread of viruses in both small and large populations.  The results of the case studies highlight the critical importance of NPIs in preventing the spread of viruses, in addition to the negative consequences of spreading rumors on the health of the population.  The model's analysis also suggests several proactive strategies to combat the spread of viruses, including the selection of key individuals to influence in order to prevent the spread of viruses in the population. We examine the effectiveness of applying a coherent state amplitude screen to the incoming signal, followed by a unitary joint measurement with assistance from a coherent catalyst, to extract classical information from the signal while maintaining security. Our investigation focuses on two scenarios: (i) the signal arrives promptly, allowing for a two-party joint measurement, and (ii) the signal has undergone significant degradation, rendering a two-party joint measurement impractical. In scenario (i), we identify the throned region where SPS yields positive output and assess its classical and semi-classical versions. In scenario (ii), we explore SPS in a truncated Wigner approximation, revealing the emergence of a stable, high-intensity output field. Notably, the parameters that maintain a stable output field within the throned region serve as guidelines for implementing SPS in experimental setups. In both scenarios, SPS exhibits a marked improvement over no subtraction, especially when the initial entanglement rate is elevated. However, it falls short in the regime where the signal entanglement rate is substantial, at which point over-cloning becomes prevalent, and photon pair production dominates. The analysis also extends to continuous spontaneous phase matching, demonstrating that SPS yields a stable output field in this case as well. The study of SPS in a quantum communication scenario where the signal entanglement rate is high may be applied to modeling pair production in unstable systems, such as vacuum entanglement in de Sitter space. The analysis indicates that true entanglement switchover, initially proposed in arXiv:2106.13631, is, in fact, a result of pair production rather than an independent phenomenon, and it suggests that the "hubble time" indication in arXiv:2106.13631 is, in reality, a photon detection time rather than a time scale associated with true entanglement switchover. The findings presented in this research have significant implications for an in-depth analysis of true entanglement switchover in arXiv:2106.13631, as well as for developing SPS in experimental setups and understanding the dynamics of continuous spontaneous phase matching, pair production in unstable systems, and the effects of photon pair production on a quantum communication channel. A significant finding from the analysis is the identification of distinct, geographically bounded areas within the studied region, where mobility behavior differs substantially from surrounding regions. in unsupervised learning, and density-based clustering stands out as a popular and effective method.  It is based on a connection to the underlying data distribution, where it groups points with a high density separated by points of low density.  Traditional DBSCAN relies on the estimation of local density, which is linked to the radius of a point's neighborhood.  However, this approach can be inflexible and may not accurately capture the complex and diverse geometries found in many real-world data sets.  In response, a variety of density-based clustering algorithms have been developed that substitute an equivalent measure for neighborhood size, depending on the specific method used.  Despite these variations, determining the optimal parameter that defines a point's neighborhood remains a significant challenge, as it can significantly influence the clustering results and is often considered a significant drawback of these methods.  This paper presents a novel, density-based clustering algorithm known as D2C, which bypasses the need to estimate neighborhood size by utilizing a statistical learning approach to predict the spatial variability of density across the data domain.  The resulting model enables the creation of a detailed, high-resolution density map, from which a set of diverse, dense regions can be identified and defined as distinct clusters.  In contrast to traditional DBSCAN and its variants, D2C does not require any parameter tuning and is capable of adapting to the complex geometries found in data sets, as demonstrated by our empirical evaluation using a broad range of test data.  We also compared D2C to a variety of alternative clustering algorithms, showcasing its superiority in terms of clustering accuracy, precision, and overall performance.  Furthermore, D2C is a scalable method that can efficiently process large data sets, as evident from our experiments involving real-world data sets containing thousands of data points.  The code for D2C has been made available online, offering a useful clustering solution for the broader data science community.  Beyond clustering, we enlisted D2C in a significant data analysis project, highlighting its potential in real-world applications by identifying areas of high density within a large geographic region.  This was achieved by applying D2C to a spatial data domain, as illustrated by our experiment using a subset of TIGER data, but with a notable limitation involving data compression.  As such, we recommend using a compact data representation that preserves spatial variability, such as the MDS representation discussed in Section 2.2, in conjunction with D2C for effective density-based data analysis. (5) EVO facilitates the identification of a stable regime, correlating with the improvement in test accuracy over time.  The proposed method, EVO, provides a customizable time-dependent energy landscape, enabling users to specify a preferred set of experiences for the network to learn from, offering vast potential for its use in deep learning, as evident in various critical applications. Analyzing the matter distribution at different redshifts, we calculated the cross-correlation of galaxy groups with their own velocity vectors and a background density field, and found that these galaxy groups exhibit enhanced mass growth in the range of scales from 1.5 to 5 times $8\times 10^{22} \, \mbox{kg}$, specifically showing an exponential development from redshift 4 to the present day.  We also observed a shift towards the formation of more massive galaxy groups as redshift decreases, with a power-law distribution that varies with redshift but remains consistent across all scales studied.  A notable finding is the alignment of the mass growth of galaxy groups on larger scales, which, on scales exceeding $10^{24} \, \mbox{kg}$, exhibits a universal pattern across all redshift values, in contrast to smaller scales that exhibit diversity across redshift levels.  We further analyzed the distribution of galaxy groups within their surrounding dark matter halos and found that they primarily reside on the edges of these halos, specifically in the vast, less dense outskirts, and have a tendency to form in the halos of already existing galaxy groups, demonstrating the tendency for galaxy groups to merge through the consumption of halos rather than groups themselves colliding.  We propose that the mass growth of these open-ended galaxy groups can be explained by the collapse of surrounding halos, supported by the observed relationship with the cross-correlation of galaxy groups with a background density field, and suggest that the study of galaxy groups in a $w w_0$ dark energy universe holds valuable insights into the evolution of massive structures in a universe dominated by a variable dark energy component.  We also outline the necessity for further research into the galactic winds, active galactic nuclei feedback, and mass distribution patterns that influence the formation of galaxy groups.   approach to addressing some of physics' open questions, such as explaining the 
  hierarchy between the electroweak and Planck scales. However, achieving a 
  comprehensive understanding of these extensions calls for a thorough analysis 
  of their fundamental phenomena, particularly in a quantum field theory context. 
  This research delves into the study of conical singularities in (1+3)-dimensional 
  space-time to determine the causal structure of a massive scalar field's quantum 
  state within an extended scalar theory, taking into account self-interaction and 
  a specific type of non-linear interaction with a vector field. This investigation 
  is part of a broader examination of the quantum state of a scalar field in an (1+3)-dimensional space-time, which has a conical singularity and is subject to certain boundary conditions, with its self-interaction described by a $\phi^3$ potential and its interaction with a massless vector field modeled through a Fermi point interaction. 
  The causal structure of this quantum state is determined by solving a set of 
  Heisenberg's equations in a complex time framework and verifying the effects 
  of a timelike vector on a pair of spacelike vectors being orthogonal. 
  The research also delves into the calculation of the quantum state's stress energy 
  tensor, specifically the mass squared boson's effective value, which is found 
  to be conformally invariant and estimated as $-2\left(\frac{1-2\gamma}{0-\gamma}\right) 
  s^2$, where $s$ represents the distance from the origin and $\gamma$ a 
  parameter dependent on the model's constants and the conical angle. 
  The analysis of a conical universe's quantum stress energy tensor is further 
  examined by modeling the universe as a closed de Sitter space rather than a 
  conical de Sitter space.

system consisting of a mobile atom interacting with a stationary background gas at low energies, a scenario known as quantum non-equilibrium dynamics. Unlike thermal equilibrium situations, this system lacks a well-established quantum regime where classical behavior dominates, often referred to as the "quantum chaos regime." In this investigation, we focus on a particular aspect - the spread of the atomic wavefunction - and examine the effects of chaos on its fluctuations. A major surprise arose during our research - the fingerprints of chaos on the wavefunction's spread exhibit an opposite behavior, increasing in the quantum regime instead of reaching a saturation point. This unusual pattern can be explained by the interference of the atomic momentum modes, particularly those with opposite momenta, which contribute positively to the fluctuations in certain quantum regimes. This phenomenon is referred to as quantum chaos revivals and it presents an novel phenomenon that can be experimentally verified using techniques like photoelectric scattering, providing insight into quantum non-equilibrium dynamics through the lens of chaos theory. To tackle this problem, we employ a combination of classical harmonic analysis and microlocal techniques to analyze the properties of solutions in the complex time-plane, specifically focusing on the behavior of solutions that exhibit soliton-like characteristics. Our analysis reveals the existence of solutions that exhibit distinct, contrasting behaviors: they may exist globally in the complex time-plane, or they may exhibit an exponential growth curve as time increases, provided that the imaginary time is sufficiently large. The results presented here also offer an alternative to the recent proofs of the soliton resolution conjecture for a third-order nonlinear Schr\"{o}dinger equation under focusing cubic nonlinearity, which were established by Chongsheng Law and Tanya, in addition to earlier works by Perelman and Zhang,  Bin, and Shen.  Our approach differs from the approach taken in our previous work, and it provides a more direct proof of the statement regarding the soliton resolution for that specific equation.  The harmonic analysis approach presented in this paper can be applied to a broader class of equations, including a generalized version of the third-order nonlinear Schr\"{o}dinger equation.  The microlocal approach, on the other hand, is specifically tailored to the complex time-plane and may be applied to models with the same characteristics as the model studied here.  The results presented in this paper can also be applied to study the dynamics of solutions that exhibit the same blow-up dynamics as the classical, large-time blow-up of the focusing cubic nonlinear Schr\"{o}dinger equation equation in the physical time-plane.  The results and approaches presented in this paper are also relevant to a wide range of other mathematical models, including the Korteweg-de Vries equation, the cubic nonlinear wave equation, the Klein-Gordon equation, the nonlinear heat equation, and the Beauvoir equation, among others.  The purpose and scope of this paper is to provide a comprehensive overview of the monodromy problem and the microlocal analysis approach to studying the dynamics of solutions to a third-order nonlinear singular Schr\"{o}dinger equation under focusing cubic nonlinearity, and to situate the main results presented in this paper within the existing body of literature on this topic, in addition to presenting a series of open questions related to the monodromy problem. By examining a representative of all galaxies where we can see the formation of stars and the elements created by them, researchers were able to test models of the formation of the interstellar medium and the elements found in young stars.  Comparing the metallicity of the interstellar medium to the elements found in young stars in the galaxy Messier 33 revealed significant differences in certain elements, particularly those with masses between 1.4 and 3.4 times that of helium.  To better understand these differences, researchers created a mathematical model of the interstellar medium and the elements found in young stars in Messier 33, relying on observations of this galaxy. Further supported by high-energy observations, enhanced formation rates of certain elements in Messier 33 are likely the result of massive star formation, while the metallicity of the interstellar medium influences the formation of other elements.  This research has implications for the study of metallicity in distant galaxies.  Further studies of galaxies like the galaxy Messier 33 are essential for a comprehensive understanding of the elements within which we see the formation of stars and the elements created by them.  To that end, researchers propose a new hypothesis for the formation of elements in the galaxy Messier 33, stemming from observations across the galaxy and incorporating the formation of elements in the interstellar medium, the metallicity of this medium, the formation of elements in the winds of massive stars, the death of these stars, and the distribution of these elements in the galaxy. call for automated data analysis, leading to a growing interest in using computational methods to examine and interpret large data sets.  As a result, researchers are now using automated tools to discover new insights in the same way they use manual methods, raising important questions about the nature of scientific discovery and how it should be reported.  This study employs a novel approach that combines automated exploration with explicit guidelines to prioritize significant findings, demonstrating our approach's effectiveness with a previously inconclusive data set.  We were able to identify key variables, develop a model, and obtain meaningful results that replicate previous studies.  Our study illustrates the potential benefits and challenges of using automated tools for data analysis, including issues of reproducibility and validation.  We found that automated analysis can yield valuable insights but may also lead to methodological difficulties, particularly in validating results.  We discovered that automated regression could lead to overly complex models, produce biased estimates, and result in models that overfit data.  We suggest that using automated tools in research requires rigorous validation procedures and encourages researchers to employ multiple validation methods.  We propose that, in addition to statistical validation, researchers should also employ conceptual validation to ensure that the discovered relationships make theoretical sense.  We believe that, with appropriate validation, automated research can significantly enhance our understanding and accurately reveal previously hidden patterns.  We were able to achieve conceptual validation with our sensor-augmented research data by comparing results to existing theories and previously unexplained empirical findings, and found that our models accurately replicated both.  We were able to achieve statistical validation by comparing estimates to previously known parameters and found that our models produced estimates within a 10% margin of error.  We were also able to achieve validation through empirical replication by using our models to make predictions and found that they held true in subsequent time periods.  We were able to achieve validation through contrast cases by comparing results from cases that should yield different outcomes and found that they did.  We were able to achieve validation through manipulation of independent variables by changing conditions that should yield different outcomes and found that they did.  We were able to achieve validation through manipulation of dependent variables by checking for reverse effects and found that they did not.  We were able to achieve validation through control variables by controlling for variables that could yield different outcomes and found that they did not.  We were able to achieve validation through hold-out samples by using our models to make predictions on unknown cases and found that they held true.  We were able to achieve validation through multiple operationalizations by using different measures of the same concept

This category includes neural networks that generate multi-dimensional vectors as output, such as attention-based networks, graph learning networks, and recurrent networks, among others. , mobile applications have significantly increased, leading to a rise in demands for wireless data services.  As a result, there is a growing interest in expanding to multi-hop wireless networks, enabling devices to act as routers and extend the coverage of the network.  This development creates opportunities for cost-efficient designs to provide wide-area coverage through a small number of range-extender routers and many access devices.  In contrast to traditional networks, multi-hop wireless networks lack standardized protocols, leading to a need for innovative protocol designs that can be applied across various network topologies.  Furthermore, the proliferation of IoT applications in these networks highlights the importance of considering device-to-device communication and routing protocols that prioritize delay-sensitive applications.  In this research, a novel routing protocol called Time-Reversed Multi-Hop Wireless Network Routing (TRMWNR) is proposed, which employs a Time-Reversed framework to detect and prevent routing loops and handle packet prioritization for delay-sensitive applications.  The design of TRMWNR was evaluated through simulations and showed improved performance in packet delivery ratio, end-to-end delay, and throughput per unit area in comparison to existing routing protocols for IoT applications in multi-hop wireless networks.  The results of the simulation demonstrated that TRMWNR exhibits enhanced robustness in time stability, network throughput, and spatial coverage in simulation scenarios.  The design of TRMWNR was considered and compared with three categories of routing protocols in the network: traditional, delay-aware, and randomized protocols.  The design of TRMWNR is applicable to a wide range of IoT applications in multi-hop wireless networks and can be implemented using a variety of data transmission protocols such as IEEE 802.15.4g.  The code of TRMWNR is available at https://github.com/JianKong/TRMWNR.  The future developments of TRMWNR include the extension of TRMWNR to mesh networks and a large-scale testbed to evaluate the design of TRMWNR in real-world scenarios. By leveraging the uniqueness of invariant measures for these operators and the ergodicity of their associated semiflows, we demonstrate the existence of a unique invariant measure for which the measure of the interior of the manifold is maximal.  Furthermore, we find that this maximal measure is stationary under the flow generated by the original nonlocal diffusion operator.  The key components of our proof involve establishing the existence of a global attractor for a family of measures, demonstrating the uniqueness of a maximal invariant measure, and using the ergodicity of the semiflow to characterize this measure as a stationary measure with maximal interior.  The nontrivial stationary measures for which the interior of the manifold is maximal can be determined through the application of Poincar\'e's variational principle to an appropriate class of compact subsets of the measure space.   using neural network Hamiltonians. A case study with a biomolecular simulation showcases 
  the method's potential, along with a key finding that a longer-cut-off cutoff scheme 
  can significantly reduce required simulations while maintaining precision. This approach has 
  significant implications for a wide range of simulations that rely on machine-learning 
  Hamiltonians, including but not limited to biomolecular simulations.  We have open-sourced

The iTHAC architecture employs a variable number of processing elements, each executing basic arithmetic operations, and a set of memory elements that manage variable sharing. We assessed the iTHAC complex arithmetic version's performance for calculating the GCD in both theoretical and experimental terms. Theoretical analysis yielded an iTHAC implementation with a time complexity of O(n^3) and a memory complexity of O(n), while comparative evaluations against the iTHAC simple arithmetic version revealed an iTHAC complex arithmetic implementation offering a 2-fold performance improvement for calculations involving two variables, and a 5-fold improvement for calculations involving three variables. Experimental data also demonstrated the iTHAC complex arithmetic version's performance when calculating the GCD in variables ranging from two to seven. is an emerging technique for synthetic data generation.  It is based on a neurodensity estimator that produces a 3D density field and a two-stream neural network that projects input images and calculates densities and ray path contributions.  While training NeRF on real images results in realistic outcomes, it requires substantial computation and memory.  Our novel framework, Real-World NeRF (RW-NeRF), bypasses the need for actual image data during training NeRF.  It is built on the premise that 3D real-world scenes remain largely unchanged, thus allowing RW-NeRF to utilize rendered images from a previous training session as real data.  The distinction between RW-NeRF and traditional methods lies in using low-frequency rendered images to train NeRF, which yields notable improvements over existing methods by limiting 3D density interpolation and enabling substantial speedup without compromise in synthesis quality.  Furthermore, RW-NeRF demonstrates unparalleled performance when working with limited-view data and a single camera, outperforming competitors by a significant margin.  Our approach also extends to handling dynamic scenes by integrating motion information into the density estimator, which leads to superior results over existing methods along with a notable reduction in computation and memory requirements.  Our RW-NeRF is relatively straightforward, yet it offers a point of departure for more complex models that can be created by integrating RW-NeRF with other NeRF-based techniques.  We have open-sourced RW-NeRF, encouraging further development and modification of this framework.  Our findings are accompanied by a comprehensive dataset containing low-frequency rendered images from actual real-world scenes, which can be utilized for training and evaluation purposes.  This dataset is notable for utilizing two novel, previously unexplored training data sources: real images and 3D density fields, which facilitates the study of the impact of training data on NeRF in relation to density field interpolation, thus allowing for a deeper understanding of RW-NeRF and NeRF in general.  Our results demonstrate the innovative capabilities of RW-NeRF across various scenarios with an accompanying 3D visu-alization and quantitative evaluation presented in the form of a video and an extensive comparison with competing methods presented in the main text.  This research paves the way for utilizing RW-NeRF as a building block to enhance the performance of NeRF by limiting 3D density interpolation, which can be achieved without a substantial increase in computation and memory requirements.  This was shown in the comparison with an internally developed NeRF baseline, which revealed a notable speedup

  framework for inferring unknown parameters in dynamic systems from a set of

  tracking error to characterize the distinction between diverse experimental 
  outcomes. By formulating the tracking error as a learning-from-examples problem, 
  the TELDE framework enables the development of a data-driven, parameter-estimation 
  model. This model can be trained to accurately predict parameters across a wide 
  range of experiments, even those conducted at a different scale. A key benefit 
  of the TELDE framework is its ability to effectively utilize a wide array of 
  experimental data, including those conducted at a larger scale, which are 
  typically difficult to analyze manually. Through a case study and numerical 
  experiments, the TELDE framework demonstrates its utility in recovering system 
  parameters from low-resolution experiments and its capacity to handle a broad 
  spectrum of high-resolution experiments.  The evaluation results show that the 
  TELDE framework yields estimation accuracy for system parameters, outperforming 
  alternative methods.  The TELDE framework's code is available at https://github.com/YuewangResearch/TELDE.

Furthermore, we investigated the risciness of a subset of these programs in the presence of additive noise, and demonstrated how the risciness is influenced by the programs' underlying dynamics when this noise is increased. Finally, we presented a strategy for reducing the risciness of a subset of these programs by applying a form of output feedback, and explored the feasibility of this strategy when the programs' underlying dynamics exhibit sensitive dependence on their initial conditions. Moreover, we investigated the practical implications of the risciness of binary integer programs subject to random causes of chaos through the solution of a management problem under uncertainty, and demonstrated how the risciness influences the optimal decision-making in this problem. A key aspect of this evaluation is identifying the most elementary grid required to replicate a specific function, which is referred to as the optimal uniform complexity or EUH complexity for short.  This concept was introduced by Paish and Toll, who demonstrated the existence of a most elementary grid that could replicate any polynomial function through a general approach, although this approach is not efficient for particular functions like x^100.  In this research, we developed a more streamlined approach to determine the EUH complexity for a range of polynomial functions, which includes x^100 as a notable example.  Our strategy involves a key innovation where we first establish a connection between the EUH complexity and the intrinsic properties of these polynomial functions, which we refer to as their harmonic decay.  This harmonic decay property serves as the primary criterion to establish the EUH complexity for a broad category of polynomial functions, offering a more direct and computationally efficient assessment of these functions' underlying complexities.  Beyond its application in determining the EUH complexity for polynomial functions, our research also introduces a novel harmonic analysis, which is a natural extension of the discrete harmonic analysis recently presented by the Harmonic Analysis Group.  This new harmonic analysis is noteworthy for utilizing a set of basis functions that are individually easy to evaluate, making it particularly useful for a wide range of applications in computer science, including geometric computation, algorithmic programming, and more.  Our research is accompanied by an open-source code developed using the Julia programming language, which is designed to automatically generate the optimal grids required to replicate various functions at the lowest possible EUH complexity, along with a range of examples highlighting its applicability.  This code is part of a larger project dedicated to the study of harmonic systems, which encompasses a wide range of phenomena governed by the harmonic decay property and presents opportunities for potential collaborations.  The key aspects of our research are also illustrated through a series of animated visuals, which are available on the Harmonic Decay Exhibition website. involves identifying the level of adversarial noise that masquerades within a dataset, rendering it ineffective for modeling. This noise is often considered part of an underlying uncertainty distribution, which significantly affects modeling performance and boosts the risk of subsequent machine learning systems. This paper introduces a novel framework, called NoiseScore, which detects this adversarial noise by leveraging the discrepancy between smooth and non-smooth functions prevalent in modern machine learning. NoiseScore generates multiple perturbation samples for each data point, representing both smooth and non-smooth distributions, and classifies noisy data as such when observed perturbations exceed an established threshold. This threshold is determined through a minimax hyperplane that differentiates normal and noisy data across the learned high-dimensional space. Experimental evaluations conducted across various datasets and non-smooth distributions, including those generated by state-of-the-art adversarial attacks, demonstrate NoiseScore's effectiveness in identifying data polluted by adversarial noise.  A detailed analysis reveals that NoiseScore complements existing preprocessing methods and facilitates enhanced modeling performance by curating clean datasets.  A theoretical analysis confirming the accuracy of NoiseScore is also presented.  This accuracy is gauged by a recently introduced metric that assesses the similarity between distributions, indicating that NoiseScore's predictions are reliable and stable over time.  Furthermore, NoiseScore's hypotheses are validated through additional experimental evaluations, showcasing its applicability across a broad spectrum of machine learning architectures and datasets.  A comparative evaluation highlights NoiseScore's innovative features that set it apart from competing noise detection solutions.  A step-by-step guide is provided to facilitate the implementation of NoiseScore, along with previously unseen results highlighting its robustness in high-stakes, real-world scenarios.  This research paves the way for further advancements in robust machine learning, enabling the development of more resilient models capable of withstanding both known and unknown types of data noise.  A preliminary outline of NoiseScore's potential applications is presented, along with previously unexplored directions for future work, such as integrating NoiseScore with existing preprocessing solutions and enhancing its scalability for large-scale dataset curating.  A set of open-source tools and code is made available to facilitate the reproduction of experimental results and further advancements in NoiseScore. Enhanced Ventilation Effectiveness Experiment, a study conducted in a sealed chamber with 1.04 billion air molecules. The experiment focused on a under-explored ventilation efficiency phenomenon - when a chamber is stirred in a perpendicular direction to its largest dimension. To analyze the ventilation effectiveness, we used two measurement methods: a simple formula and a more complex computational model. The results showed that a commonly used formula overestimates the ventilation effectiveness, especially in the most frequently used chamber configurations. A significant area with low ventilation effectiveness was discovered in the central region of the chamber and we propose a new formula to describe this region. The central region's ventilation effectiveness can be influenced by the stirring speed, but it has no impact on the effectiveness of the surrounding areas. The results of the experiment and simulation were validated by measuring the concentrations of two substances released into the chamber during three separate experiments. Subject to certain conditions on the potential energy, this approximation yields an exponentially decayed series with a compact support equal to the original problem's fundamental domain. In contrast to the standard Gaussian-based approximation, this method does not require the assumption that the potential energy be short-range and instead allows for an iterative process to determine the coefficients of the approximation series. Moreover, this approach enables the derivation of an inequality characterizing the remainder of the series in terms of the remainder of the potential energy, thereby establishing the compactness of the series' support. A relevant example is also presented to demonstrate the advantages of this method over the traditional approach. These findings suggest that this step function-based approximation presents several practical benefits for solving both theoretical and experimental problems related to the time-independent Schr\"{o}dinger equation with periodic boundary conditions.  An important application of this method is shown in the paper's appendix.  To the best of our knowledge, this approach has not been previously reported in the mathematical literature.  We believe that these results have value for both theoretical and experimental studies of the time-independent Schr\"{o}dinger equation with periodic boundary conditions.  An application of these findings to the study of approximate eigenfunctions of the time-independent Schr\"{o}dinger equation with a Krahmanov-Petkovny class potential near the Fermi level of solid state physics is also explored in the paper's appendix. Our work yields a set of conditions under which these matrix norms exhibit specific behaviors, providing a foundation for developing algorithms that utilize matrix norms in dynamic graphs. Our contributions offer a range of possibilities for further enhancements. }  In the context of a variable graph $G$ with vertex set $V$ and edge set $E$, we define the adjacency matrix norm $\|A\|_{G}$ and the Laplacian matrix norm $\|L\|_{G}$. Our main results hold under the assumption that the graph $G$ satisfies certain connectivity properties, which we refer to as $\kappa$-connectedness for a given parameter $\kappa$. Leveraging these matrix norms, we establish the inequality $\|L\|_{\mathcal{G}}} \newcommand{\N}{\mathcal{N}"} \leq 2\kappa \|A\|_{\mathcal{G}}}$, which facilitates an exploration of the relationship between the Laplacian matrix norm and the adjacency matrix norm in $\kappa$-connected graphs. Our research also delves into the connection between these matrix norms and the spectral embedding, shortest paths, and connectivity properties of graphs. By examining the Laplacian matrix norm in a specific type of graph, we gain insights into the relationship between the largest eigenvalue of the Laplacian matrix and the distance between adjacent vertices. Our findings indicate that the Laplacian matrix norm dominates the geometric property of graphs, offering a matrix-based representation that captures the essence of this graph property. As such, we believe that our results have a degree of generality and can be applied to a broader category

  offering a flexible framework that accommodates various transmission models, such as

  stable behavior. Furthermore, we demonstrate the existence of periodic solutions

  observed in a classic discrete dynamical system. The research also touches upon

  systems, using a geometric approach to describe the distribution of periodic
  solutions at different stages of the bifurcation diagram. The paper further
  delves into a real-world application, modeling a recent measles outbreak in
  the United States using the delayed transmission model and analyzing the
  epidemiological impact of delayed transmissions. The study encourages future
  research into the dynamics of delayed transmission models, particularly the
  periodic solutions that may have crucial implications for prediction and control
  purposes, using the considered case study of measles outbreak as an example.

  vaccine recipients and compares their frequencies to those in unvaccinated 
  individuals. A retrospective analysis of 20 million people in five European 
  countries who were eligible for the AstraZeneca vaccine revealed that between 
  January 24th and March 24th, 3.2 million individuals were inoculated with the 
  vaccine. Compared to unvaccinated individuals, those who received the vaccine 
  had a 0.69 times higher odds of experiencing a cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, 
  with a estimated incidence rate of 2.14 per million vaccinated individuals, 
  and a 1.53 times higher odds of experiencing an intracranial hemorrhage, with 
  an estimated incidence rate of 5.7 per million vaccinated individuals. Although 
  the incidence rates of these disorders in vaccinated individuals are subject to 
  change as more data becomes available, the current estimates suggest that 
  cerebral venous sinus thrombosis and intracranial hemorrhage occur at rates 
  10 to 30 times lower than myocardial infarction and at rates similar to those 
  of pulmonary embolism. Consequently, the benefits of the AstraZeneca vaccine 
  in preventing COVID-19-related deaths likely outweigh its risks in the general 
  population, especially among the elderly where COVID-19-related deaths pose 
  the greatest threat.  The temporary pause in the distribution of the AstraZeneca 
  vaccine may have resulted in a delay in inoculations, leading to additional 
  deaths caused by COVID-19. Hence, it is crucial to weigh the potential benefits 
  and risks of the vaccine thoroughly before implementing vaccination protocols. 
  As the data becomes more comprehensive, ongoing research will be monitoring 
  the incidence of blood-clotting disorders in vaccinated individuals to ensure 
  the safety of the vaccine and to adjust vaccination strategies accordingly.

Neural Networks (BNNs), require
  training a network multiple times to achieve optimal performance.  BNNs, in
  particular, involve significant training efforts due to the time required to
  perform a single inference using a Monte-Carlo estimator, rendering them
  infeasible for tasks with a large number of data points.  A significant
  shortcoming of existing BNN methods is their inability to efficiently
  utilize multiple parallel GPUs, hindering their ability to process large
  datasets efficiently.  A novel BNN model has been developed that overcomes
  these limitations by utilizing a linear approximation of the network's
  posterior, thereby reducing training time and facilitating the utilization
  of parallel GPUs for large-scale data processing.  The model's posterior
  inference is framed as a linear regression problem, allowing for the use
  of efficient stochastic gradient methods that support parallelization across
  multiple GPUs, thus enabling the processing of large datasets at a much
  faster rate than previously possible.  The proposed method is referred
  to as FastBayesOpt (FBO), which includes an optimized version called
  FastBayesOpt with Noise Contrastive Estimation (FBO-NCE) and has been
  evaluated extensively across various benchmark datasets through experiments
  conducted on multiple parallel GPUs, revealing its superior performance. 
  The code for FBO has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/
  TencentMTC/FastBayesOpt. 
  The evaluation of FBO-NCE across real-world datasets, including CIFAR-100
  and ImageNet, showed its capabilities for handling massive datasets with a
  relatively small number of models, taking only a tenth of the typical
  training time while achieving comparable accuracy levels. 
  The proposed FBO-NCE model has several key innovations including an
  approximate posterior inference framework that leverages a linear
  representation, an optimized stochastic gradient descent method with a
  parallelization strategy across multiple GPUs, and a built-in regularizer
  mechanism that prevents overfitting, thus enabling the efficient training
  of BNNs on large datasets. 
  The developed FBO-NCE model has several practical applications in the
  field of machine learning, specifically in the realm of BNNs with an
  abundance of parallel GPUs for the processing of large datasets at a fast
  rate without sacrificing accuracy levels. 
  The code for FBO-NCE has been made available on GitHub

To evaluate the automatic analysis capabilities of these networks, the research introduces a novel framework that assesses their ability to identify long-distance relationships in randomly generated sentence pairs, lacking any semantic connection. This framework enables the examination of neural network performance across various linguistic long-distance phenomena, such as relative clauses, object extraction, and subject-verb agreement, which involve complex syntactic and semantic interactions. A key discovery reveals that neural networks can analyze the sequence structure to discern meaningful information from distant parts of the input, even in semantically unrelated contexts, although they frequently confuse related patterns, especially when the underlying relationships are complex, and when the associated words are distant from each other. In evaluating the capacity of neural networks to process linguistic long-distance phenomena in actual sentences, the study demonstrates that while they exhibit a certain level of performance consistency, this is significantly surpassed by their ability to settle through sequence structure analysis, making this a crucial aspect in accounting for their success. The research data is openly accessible at: https://parsonage.github.io/reveal-long-distance/. The code for the experiments is available at: https://github.com/parsonage/reveal-long-distance. The underlying hypothesis of the study assumes that the internal understanding of neural networks can be represented graphically, which the study verifies through an innovative visualization method called path sampling. The proposed method can be utilized to develop a more precise sequence-to-sequence training dataset, along with a descriptive framework for long-distance relationships in the ADVENT tree schema. The study also explores multiple quantitative assessments that consider the relationships' depth, remoteness, and the presence of intervening entities or operations, such as relative clause formation, where the study employs a novel technique called tree transformation matching to automate the annotation process. The research further delves into the analysis of a recently introduced dataset called CLS-SANT through the same lenses, revealing a more intricate structure where the beginning and end of the involved spans are processed separately. The study demonstrates that the capability of neural networks to process long-distance relationships within actual sentences is significantly more intricate and depends largely on the underlying syntax, semantics, and specific phenomena in question. Generally, neural networks are trained to achieve high accuracy despite being prone to deviations in input data, such as image distortions caused by lighting variations, misclassifying certain data points despite, and the need for networks to be protected against malicious data manipulations.

This impossibility stems from the incompatibility of two fundamental principles: thermalization must occur in a manner that respects the second law of thermodynamics, and the deterministic evolution of a Hamiltonian system must adhere to Liouville's theorem. This incompatibility is reflected in a mathematical contradiction that arises when attempting to construct a demon utilizing a microcanonical ensemble. The resulting contradiction is analogous to a version of the halting problem, indicating that there is no universal strategy for creating an efficient demon. Consequently, Maxwell's demon can only function by relying on a specific, artificial source of entropy, contradicting the original intention. This finding also provides a new perspective on the relationship between the second law of thermodynamics and the limits of computational processes, offering insights into the fundamental constraints that govern both natural and artificial systems. This research is based on a recent understanding facilitated by a graphical representation of microcanonical ensembles. The interconnection between the variables of a system through conserved quantities is revealed through a set of coupled equations, revealing the impossibility for a demon to exploit both position and momentum information simultaneously. The robustness of this conclusion is examined through the lens of three artificial scenarios: a harmonic oscillator, a Calabi-Yau manifold, and a general quasi-integrable system. The fundamental constraint that renders Maxwell's demon ineffective is shown to stem directly from the topological characteristics of these ensembles. The inapplicability of a demon to natural systems is demonstrated by the calculation of entropy production rates, which are found to be positive and determined by the interaction between the system and its environment, reflecting the irreversible dissipation of energy through scattering processes. The impossibility of a demon to natural systems is further highlighted by the statistical distribution of the action variable, which cannot be skewed to generate a thermal gradient. The possibility of creating a demon is examined for artificial systems through the addition of a tiny source of chaos by perturbing a quasi-integrable system, revealing that even in such cases, the entropy production remains positive and cannot be harnessed to generate a thermal gradient. The fundamental limitation of a demon to natural systems is shown to be marked by the invariance of topological invariants, such as the area of the microcanonical ensemble, which cannot decrease in a natural process. The consequences of this understanding for the limits of computational processes are examined, revealing that even the most efficient algorithms will always generate a positive entropy, which is determined by the complexity of the underlying dynamics. This method is known as Wi-Fi geo-location, a term used here to encompass all similar techniques using layer two and three signals for position determination.  Research in this field focuses on improving the accuracy of Wi-Fi geo-location through signal analysis, presenting several methods to create maps of location to signal strength, often referred to as fingerprinting databases.  These databases can be based on a single time period or they can dynamically update to reflect changes in signal patterns over time.  This research investigated three techniques for creating such databases: spatial, temporal, and spatial-temporal models, using Wi-Fi signals from mobile devices in an airport setting.  The results showed that while considering the movement of devices over time improves the accuracy of Wi-Fi geo-location, this method's limitations, especially in terms of memory usage, make it crucial to find a balance in its application.  This balance can be achieved by giving priority to temporal models for areas with low spatial coverage, such as airports, and reserving spatial-temporal models for areas with high spatial coverage, such as indoor environments.  The evaluation of these models across an airport setting revealed that while they require a significant amount of storage, they can significantly improve the accuracy of Wi-Fi geo-location, thus they are suitable for indoor environments but may not be suitable for applications with data storage limitations such as the airport scenario studied here.  Alternative solutions for such environments may involve continuous updates of static temporal models or using gradient descent to dynamically adjust the parameters of these models.  The positive aspect of these approaches is that they do not require a significant amount of storage, thus they have the potential to be used in various applications including the airport scenario studied here.  The pros and cons of these approaches along with their implementation details are discussed in the conclusion section along with possible future works.  The airport dataset used in this research is available for public use, thus it may be useful for testing and evaluating other similar approaches in the future. Presently, GNNs lack an effective strategy to address this common data deficiency issue. In contrast to traditional feedforward networks, GNNs' propensity to exploit neighboring information makes them poorly equipped to handle missing data. This issue is particularly pronounced in dynamic graphs with constantly evolving node features. In this work, we introduce a novel framework, called MBR-GNN, which employs a batch-reconstruction technique to enhance the robustness of GNNs to noisy and missing data. The MBR-GNN framework comprises a BGGNN encoder that uses a stochastic neighbor selection method to generate a subsample of relevant nodes, followed by a feature refiner that corrects the prediction output by eliminating artificial components created during forward propagation. We demonstrate the MBR-GNN framework's robustness benefits through experiments on numerous graph classification and node classification datasets, with MBR-GNN outperforming a range of robust GNN baselines across the board. When the outer cylinder is subjected to a pressure drop, fluid moves out of the inner cylinder, mimicking the way air leaves the body under changing pressure.  By testing different cylinder sizes and observing how mass transfers between the inner and outer cylinders, researchers can develop a useful model to predict decompression sickness in the body.  This study analyzed how mass transfer changes when the inner cylinder is stationary or rotating, which affects transfer on its surface.  Experimental results showed that mass transfer increases with increased rotation and pressure drop, and is influenced by the space between the inner and outer cylinders.  However, this study did not account for another important factor, mass that sticks to the inner cylinder surface, which can stay there and slowly leave the body.  Based on the findings, a model of mass transfer was developed that can be applied to a variety of composite cylinders, including those in scuba diving. A new study focuses on carbon bilayer and triblayer materials, incorporating theoretical models to predict how layering affects the spatial distribution of excitons and thus their physical properties, including boomerang excitons and layer-specific interactions.   where high-quality annotated data are used to train models that subsequently annotate new data in their own right. 
  This approach has shown significant gains in several classification tasks. 
  However, the underlying theory has yet to be fully understood. 
  To address this knowledge gap, we conducted an in-depth analysis of user-centered annotation's effectiveness 
  using a simplified framework focused on regression tasks. 
  The results revealed that the efficacy of user-centered annotation can be attributed to 
  a key phenomenon called "distribution smoothing". 
  In essence, the annotation process averages the original data distributions, 
  which in turn boosts the performance on unrelated tasks with overlapping distributions. 
  The findings from our linear and nonlinear experiments demonstrated that, 
  while nonlinear models can exhibit non-average behaviors, 
  the primary driving force behind their success remains the distribution smoothing effect. 
  To better illustrate and generalize these findings, 
  we introduced a theoretical model called "smoothing spectrum" 
  to describe the degree to which different distributions contribute to a common outcome. 
  The subsequent analysis of this model facilitated valuable insights, 
  such as identifying the conditions under which user-centered annotation is particularly beneficial, 
  as well as indicating that using diverse distributions leads to improved performance. 
  The proposed framework is accompanied by empirical studies and numerical calculations, 
  which helped us derive practical strategies for enhancing the diversity of smoothed distributions, 
  in turn promoting the performance gains achieved through user-centered annotation. 
  The introduced ideas are applicable across various machine learning tasks, 
  providing a theoretical foundation for understanding the annotation methods' effectiveness. 
  The code for our experiments is available at https://github.com/ryousai/smoothing_spectra.

As a rule-based system, CLIP enables the creation of new concepts by combining existing ones, a feature we leveraged to develop a large, general set of policy proposals.  By applying these concepts to suitable, high-stakes text datasets, we generated an extensive collection of 200,000 unique policy proposals.  To evaluate the quality of these proposals, we conducted a survey among 3,000 participants from 150 countries, asking them to rate a subset of 10,000 proposals on their utility in addressing global problems.  The resulting ratings were utilized to train a model that ranked proposals on their practical value, allowing us to position our initial proposals along a spectrum of rising utility as shown in Figure 1.  The learned values were also utilized to train a language model that employed the value information to enhance performance in a variety of tasks, demonstrating improvements in classification, sentiment analysis, and language generation tasks due to the inherently positive or negative phrasing associated with certain concepts.  The code, datasets, and models are available at https://policyhub.github.io/.  A related paper on modifying the CLIP framework to incorporate the value of concepts was also presented in arXiv 2208.05695. Note that the copyright for the original text datasets remains with their respective owners.  The proposed approach can be utilized to develop specialized sets of policy proposals for particular domains by employing domain-specific text datasets.  The utility ratings and associated models can be employed to enhance the performance of language models on tasks involving positive or negative phrasing.  The proposed framework has several practical applications, including serving as a foundation for developing new, domain-specific proposals or enhancing the performance of language models in classifications influenced by the positiveness or negation of certain phrases.  The results demonstrate that pre-training a language model on proposals alongside the associated value information yields a significant improvement in performance on a variety of tasks, surpassing the performance of a baseline model pre-trained on text datasets without value information by an average of 10% as shown in Figure 2.  The proposed approach to determining the value of proposals is scalable, enabling the evaluation of large, general sets of proposals. rely heavily on the 
  efficient operation of UDP-based applications and IP networks. This research 
  focuses on an underexplored aspect of UDP, specifically its congestion 
  control mechanisms, to analyze the effects of an emerging technique called 
  UDP congestion control. This approach, found in various devices and some 
  operating systems, mistakenly assumes UDP's original intention and behaves 
  similarly to TCP. Contrary to general perceptions, the original RFC 7627 
  specifies that UDP should not be used for reliable connections or flow 
  control, instead emphasizing its role in allowing higher layer protocols 
  to make informed sending decisions. As a result, our study highlights the 
  critical difference between the standard and an erroneous interpretation 
  of UDP, as well as the implications for an emerging class of applications 
  and an increasing number of networked devices with flawed congestion control 
  mechanisms. These devices can cause problems for an application that 
  sends large amounts of data at a constant rate, such as struggling to 
  establish connections with certain servers or experiencing severe performance 
  issues in certain network conditions. To address these issues, our research 
  proposes an optimized strategy called ORCA that addresses issues like 
  connection establishment delays, performance degradation in fast-mobility 
  scenarios, and an significant performance improvement in constant-bitrate 
  scenarios. Our results demonstrate the benefits of ORCA in various scenarios 
  and highlight an important consideration for an emerging class of devices 
  and an critical need for further standardization efforts to clarify the 
  behavior of UDP congestion control. Additionally, our research provides an 
  open-source implementation of ORCA for an specific type of device and 
  an idea for an simple modification that an major operating system 
  distribution could implement. Furthermore, our research highlights an 
  opportunity for an already standardized technique called UDP congestion 
  control to enhance an emerging class of applications and an critical need 
  for further research on an already validated approach called delayed 
  transition detection.

a single introduction of the SARS-CoV-2 virus is known as the basic reproduction number (R0). Estimating R0 in the early stages of a pandemic is critical for predicting disease trajectory and informing public health policy, but it is challenging to determine reliably. A study collected and analyzed 137 estimates of R0 from 18 countries and territories during the initial three months of their respective pandemics. It discovered a pattern of R0 decreasing over time in almost all regions, which was found to be explainable by modeling time changes. This model was used to study the variability across different areas and it became clear that R0 initially varied significantly across these regions but eventually converged. In contrast, the model highlighted the complexities of R0's temporal dynamics in each region, which appeared resistant to straightforward interpretation. Further analysis suggested that the primary reasons for R0's initial variability within each area were related to population size, importation of cases, temperature, and population mobility, whereas the fluctuating dynamics of R0 in each area were influenced by a variety of factors such as population mobility, temperature, rainfall, and public health measures, and these factors varied significantly across different areas. By examining the time frames in which the basic reproduction number fluctuated beyond a threshold value (greater than 1), the research identified early windows of the pandemic in each area that were characterized by rapid growth, peak growth rates, and peak case detection counts. It also became evident that these phases and time frames were largely unaccounted for in existing models and data analyses. Furthermore, the study demonstrated that first-derivative control methods can be effective in mitigating the effects of high R0 in certain areas, but to that end, monitoring of R0's temporal dynamics is necessary. The research's findings and insights are valuable for evaluating the efficacy of public health interventions in real-time and for accurately identifying high-risk periods in the pandemic in order to allocate limited resources effectively. The study's methodology can be applied to any data set from the pandemic and other outbreaks. This phenomenon has been observed in a wide range of NLP applications, including but not limited to stylometry-based fake news detection, hate speech identification using language nuances, and AI-powered healthcare text analysis.  As a result, it's essential to incorporate bias-aware techniques into NLP models to prevent the reinforcement of preexisting biases and prevent harm caused by deploying such models in real-world settings.  In this paper, a specific case study is examined where bias-aware techniques are applied to a particular NLP task known as low-stakes writing style imitation.  This task involves generating text in a particular style, such as formally or informally, without considering content.  A dataset called BERTsmall was utilized, which contains small text segments with associated sentiment labels.  Three different datasets with varying levels of sentiment were used to train separate models, each trained to recognize sentiment rather than style.  The models' ability to incorporate biases was evaluated by analyzing their ability to replicate the frequency present in the original dataset.  It was discovered that the models successfully replicated the distribution of certain labels, but failed to replicate others.  This suggests that the BERTsmall dataset is not entirely free from biases.  The paper also examined various processing techniques used in natural language processing, including but not limited to text preprocessing, removing sentiment-bearing words, and removing certain labels.  These techniques were effective in replicating certain distributions but often resulted in a decrease in accuracy.  The paper's findings indicate that even small text domains can contain biases and that deep learning models can replicate these biases.  Furthermore, removing certain words or labels may not necessarily remove the corresponding biases.  Therefore, it is crucial to carefully evaluate the effects of processing techniques on style imitation to prevent the reinforcement of preexisting biases.  Additionally, the paper proposes a critical aspect of evaluating the BERTsmall dataset, which is the consideration of domain-specific biases.  For instance, the models were found to exhibit hate speech bias when generating hate speech texts.  This highlights the significance of thoroughly examining the biases present in datasets and the resulting models, especially in areas like healthcare and social media. Assuming a signal with the same characteristics as GW14, a single detected quasiperiodic signal would yield a confidence level of 5.9σ. Among the analyzed data, we identify potential signals with a 5σ confidence level for 9 instances, and verify that these instances do not stem from non-cosmically motivated sources or instrumental anomalies. We propose a novel approach to model the harmonic components of these signals by introducing a series with unknown starting points, and demonstrate that this method yields more accurate measurements of their fundamental frequency, decay rate, and amplitude ratios. Furthermore, we develop a technique to estimate the statistical significance of these putative signals based on a proxy that accounts for the harmonic content, and employ a network of detectors to enhance the significance of the top quasiperiodic candidate by elevating its confidence level to 7.8σ following the inclusion of LIGO's 2016 January data. We do not observe a match between the detected frequencies and known terrestrial vibrations, and suggest possible connections with the recently identified rotational dynamics of supermassive black holes. We also explore the prospect of detecting quasiperiodic signals through a simplified model of their power spectrum, and investigate how future observatories will enhance the detection confidence of such signals.   is an important area of study for light-central collisions. While quarkonium production
  is primarily affected by colorless initial states, correlations in light-central collisions
  are influenced by both initial and final state interactions. This research focuses on
  calculating heavy quarkonium production at high $p_T$ in light-central collisions based
  on Color Glass Condensate (CGC) dynamics, which represents the initial state of a
  quark gluon plasma. A modified Weldon function was employed to determine the quarkonium
  state and a linearized version of the Lenaghan-Loewen-Quirk (LLQ) formula to calculate
  its momentum. A crucial factor in calculating heavy quarkonium momentum is the correct
  treatment of the gluon momentum, which is modeled as a power-law due to the unknown
  properties of the CGC dynamics. This research also accounts for the influence of a
  quark gluon plasma state on quarkonium formation by incorporating a $A_\tau$-dependent
  gluon distribution, assumed to be proportional to the saturation scale $A_{\frac{3}{2}}$.
  A numerical analysis was performed to heavy quarkonium momentum spectra, correlation
  functions, and polarization densities. The results demonstrate that while the average
  transverse momentum of heavy quarkonium may exceed 2 GeV in light-central collisions,
  the expected values for average $p_T$ vary significantly across different collisions
  energies and centralities. Furthermore, the predicted polarization densities indicate
  that heavy quarkonium polarization may be significant, especially at low momenta,
  which could be confirmed by upcoming experimental data from LHC runs at 5.02 TeV and
  39 TeV with high $p_T$ cuts, and potentially from future experiments like the Future
  Circular Collider (FCC). The research emphasizes the importance of incorporating
  initial state effects into heavy quarkonium production studies and highlights the
  need for further theoretical developments to accurately calculate the gluon momentum
  in CGC dynamics. The developed code is available at: https://github.com/hamzagarahani/cgc_quarkonium. The results presented in the research can be reproduced using the code by running the developed Python scripts. The research code has been reviewed by experts in the field of heavy quarkonium production in light-central collisions based on Color Glass Condensate dynamics

We develop a learning algorithm based on a control policy that uses relative stability as its performance metric. Relative stability indicates the ratio of the system's ability to return to equilibrium after being disrupted to the time it takes to do so. We prove that our algorithm learns a stable control policy that maximizes rewards in the presence of an unknown external force, and compare its performance to other control policies. This generalization is crucial for understanding the sensitivity of eigenvalue statistics to changes in a system's parameters. We analyze a comprehensive framework of tridiagonal matrix ensembles with Gaussian or Bernoulli entry distributions and show that the top eigenvalue's asymptotic behavior can be described by a specific stochastic process. This process depends on the specific properties of the matrix model and includes well-known processes as special cases. For example, in models with a constant second moment, the top eigenvalue's asymptotic behavior is described by a Gumbel distribution, which indicates that the largest eigenvalue will grow approximately logarithmically with the matrix's size. In contrast, models with non-constant second moments exhibit a more complex behavior, reflected in a Feller process, and can lead to a faster than logarithmic growth of the largest eigenvalue. We also derive precise probability estimates that enable us to determine the likelihood of the largest eigenvalue exceeding a particular threshold in a given large matrix. This research deepens our comprehension of the spatial statistics of eigenvalues in tridiagonal matrix ensembles and sheds light on a fundamental open question regarding the distribution of the largest eigenvalue in a Wigner matrix. 
  The findings presented in this study have significant implications for a broad category of random matrix models and provide a useful statistical framework for analyzing the stability of dynamic systems governed by Wigner matrices. 
  Furthermore, our research demonstrates that the top eigenvalue's asymptotic behavior in a Gaussian tridiagonal matrix is described by a Feller process whose stationary distribution is a two-point stationary distribution, with points at 2 and 0, respectively, indicating that in such systems the probability of the top eigenvalue exceeding 2 in a large matrix is extremely low, and it has a tendency to stabilize at a point close to 0 as the matrix grows in size. 
  This result is noteworthy as it holds under a condition on the second moment that can be verified explicitly for a wide range of tridiagonal matrix ensembles, including ensembles defined by a specific distribution with a free parameter, such as the reduced tridiagonal Gaussian unitary ensemble (GUE) or the tridiagonal Bernoulli ensemble, making it an invaluable statistical tool for studying the stability of these systems.

Specifically, topological quantum order is characterized by a topological quantum entanglement spectrum, which forms a hierarchical long-distance pattern as a result of entanglement renormalization. Our study focuses on the topological quantum order found in the Kitaev honeycomb lattice model. We demonstrate that this model's ground-state entanglement spectrum exhibits a universal hierarchical structure, which can be understood by applying the honeycomb lattice's local operators to its high-symmetry point version, the Kitaev toric code. Our analysis involves a novel, precise characterization of the toric code's entanglement spectrum's hierarchical structure, which we refer to as "penta-fusion" hierarchy. The higher-energy portion of the toric code's entanglement spectrum exhibits a simpler "fusion" hierarchy, which we previously identified. The combination of these hierarchies fully captures the topological quantum order of the Kitaev honeycomb lattice model. Our analytical findings are supported by numerical simulations. In particular, the minor discrepancies found in these simulations can be attributed to a lack of overcomplete basis for the toric code's entanglement spectrum. To accurately extract this information, jet substructure must be effectively reconstructed in heavy-ion collisions. However, due to the high levels of background and colliding velocities in these experiments, achieving reliable substructure reconstruction can be challenging. To address this difficulty, we have developed a novel substructure reconstruction approach known as the "causal enhanced filtered reconstruction" method, which employs a causal approach to eliminate background noise and utilizes a machine learning-driven filter to select jets based on their substructure characteristics. This approach has led to a significant improvement in the efficiency of jet substructure reconstruction in PbPb collisions, resulting in an enhancement of up to twenty times in reconstruction efficiency for certain jet configurations.  The enhanced filter, in particular, has been found to be highly effective in distinguishing large-radius jets in heavy-ion collisions, with a 90% efficiency in distinguishing jets based on their substructure at a 5 GeV level of significance. To further evaluate the validity of this approach, we have employed Monte Carlo simulations of proton-proton collisions, which demonstrate that this method retains its efficiency in pure hadron collision environments. With advancements in detector technology and potential increases in colliding velocities in upcoming experiments, this novel substructure reconstruction approach is poised to play a critical role in the effective extraction of quark gluon plasma properties through jet substructure analysis. The causal enhanced filtered reconstruction approach has been incorporated into the CMS experiment's jet substructure reconstruction algorithms for PbPb collisions at a 13 TeV collision energy. The enhancement of this approach is currently being utilized in the CMS experiment and is anticipated to be highly beneficial for upcoming experiments such as the CMS with a High Granularity Calorimeter at a 100 TeV collision energy. This method is applied to a specific problem where the viscosity differs depending on the distance from the origin and is modelled using a power function. A key feature of the proposed approach is the use of non-uniform mesh sizes that are tailored to the viscosity function, resulting in a well-posed problem and a convergent solution. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of the proposed approach to a problem with an interface and a power function viscosity, and provide a comparative analysis of the achieved results using different mesh sizes. Additionally, we consider a series of test cases with Dirichlet boundary conditions and an infinite domain, and show that the proposed approach yields accurate solutions compared to the analytical ones. This system of inequalities consists of the Kaletnik-type conditions adapted to finite planes, and its solutions are dependent on two parameters, $n$ and $k$. In this period, numerous thousands of exoplanetary systems have been identified, and a few hundred are thought to reside within their planet's life-friendly zone. Although numerous studies focus on detecting life on exoplanetary systems, little work has been done to explore the fate of planets within our own solar system that may have escaped into exoplanetary-like environments. In this paper, a new method has been developed to detect distant, degraded cometary remnants surrounding various exoplanetary systems using the W.M. Keck Telescope. By utilizing this method, we discovered evidence of a distant, degraded comet within the Beta Pictoris system and propose a comet scenario to explain the observed features of several other exoplanetary systems, including 55 Arietis A, Epsilon Eridani, and Fomalhout. We conclude that various exoplanetary systems may harbor similar remnants and suggest that a wide range of exoplanetary systems, including gas giant and terrestrial systems, may have comet populations fueled by a distant solar system analogue. We propose that a distant solar system, no matter its exoplanetary type, may leave behind a signature of scattered light peaked in the 520 nanometer range, which can be detected using high-resolution imaging equipped with a 10 angstroms passband filter.  The detection of a potential debris comet within the Beta Pictoris system supports recent findings from direct imaging and suggests that a prominent feature in the visible light spectrum may indicate the presence of a distant, degraded comet. The proposed method has been validated through extensive noise simulations and is accompanied by a new algorithm to detect peaked patterns in scattering. The developed method has been applied to a previously imaged list of stars and facilitated the re-detection of the Beta Pictoris system debris comet, along with tentative evidence of a second debris comet within the 55 Arietis A system. The proposed method has significant implications for understanding the fate of small bodies within solar systems beyond their planet-forming phase and has far-reaching observational and theoretical consequences.   However, annotating images for object masks is a laborious task, especially for large
  datasets with many images. This limitation tends to hinder the development of new
  methods. In response to the growing need for large, high-quality datasets, we present
  a novel unsupervised object mask annotation method called Spatially-Variant Transfer
  Learning (SVTL). SVTL's core idea is to generate object mask annotations in an unsupervised
  manner by identifying co-occurring objects within a small, locally annotated dataset.
  It achieves this through a dual-path network that simultaneously detects objects and
  classifies their masks. The network is trained to minimize the discrepancy in feature spaces
  between a large, unannotated dataset and the local annotation set, with the latter
  being weighted based on the relevance of each object to the current image.
  Experimentation with the ILSVRC dataset reveals that SVTL outperforms existing unsupervised
  object detection methods by a significant margin, with performance comparable to fully
  supervised object detection on the COCO dataset at 30% of the usual annotation scale.  We also introduce an evaluation protocol for assessing the quality of the annotations generated in an unsupervised setting, with the pre-trained model able to achieve a reasonable mAP of 24% on the ILSVRC dataset with 10% annotation coverage.  Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the SVTL-annotated datasets by fine-tuning a fully supervised object detection model on them, resulting in a significant performance boost of up to 13% mAP compared to random initialization.  The code and datasets generated using SVTL are available at https://github.com/implus/SVTL.  Note that we have re-named the method from its original title "Unsupcosed Object Detection by Co-occurring Transfer Learning" to "Spatially-Variant Transfer Learning" to reflect its connection to the CVT-LT method.
